title: Frustration
subtitle: When an unforeseen event discharges a contract nobody breached
objectives: State the test for frustration and explain why the doctrine is deliberately confined to narrow circumstances
Identify why self-induced frustration and foreseen-and-provided-for events fall outside the doctrine
Apply the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 to work out the financial consequences of a frustrating event

leadingAuthorities.role: Origin of the doctrine: destruction of the subject matter discharges the contract
Frustration of purpose — the whole point of the contract disappears, though performance remains physically possible

leadingAuthorities.citation: Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC [1956] AC 696
leadingAuthorities.role: Modern test: performance must be radically different, not merely more onerous or expensive

leadingAuthorities.citation: J Lauritzen v Wijsmuller (The Super Servant Two) [1990] 1 Lloyd's Rep 1
leadingAuthorities.role: Self-induced frustration bars reliance on the doctrine

leadingAuthorities.citation: Canary Wharf v European Medicines Agency [2019] EWHC 335 (Ch)
leadingAuthorities.role: Modern application confirming the narrowness of the doctrine, including on Brexit-related arguments

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students treat frustration as a rescue doctrine for any contract that has become a bad deal. Where the profile shows knowledge outpacing application, this note appears: 'You know the four-part test — the exam wants you to prove why it fails on facts that look tempting but aren't enough.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've got the definitions down. This lesson is weighted towards fact patterns designed to look like frustration and not be — read each scenario for what it's actually testing before answering.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush past the Taylor v Caldwell test itself — everything else in this lesson is really just qualifications and exceptions to that one core sentence.

overview.hook: A music hall is booked for two days, at a fee, to watch the King's coronation procession pass by. Then the King falls ill and the procession is cancelled. Nobody breached anything. Nobody could have stopped it. So who bears the loss? This lesson is about the doctrine that answers that question — and about how narrowly the courts have kept the door open ever since.

parts.heading: The doctrine's birth: when the thing itself is destroyed
parts.voice: historical-narrative — traces the doctrine from its founding case forward
body: Before 1863, English contract law took an unforgiving view of impossibility: a promise was a promise, and if performance became impossible through no fault of either party, that was simply the promisor's bad luck — they remained liable in damages regardless. This was called absolute contractual liability, and it produced some genuinely harsh results.

Taylor v Caldwell broke that rule. The defendants had agreed to let the claimants use a music hall for a series of concerts. Before the first concert, and without fault on either side, the hall burned down. The claimants sued for their wasted advertising expenses, arguing the contract required the defendants to provide the hall regardless of what happened to it.

The court disagreed, and in doing so created the doctrine of frustration. It held that where the continued existence of a specific thing is essential to performance, the contract is subject to an implied condition that the parties are excused if, without their fault, that thing perishes before the time for performance. The hall's destruction discharged both parties from further obligation — nobody breached, and nobody could sue for lost expectations.

Notice what this case does and does not decide. It is narrow on its own facts — physical destruction of the specific subject matter — but it plants the seed of a much bigger principle: that some supervening events are so fundamental they release both parties from a bargain neither of them broke.

components.definition: The automatic discharge of a contract where, after formation and without either party's fault, an event occurs that renders performance impossible, illegal, or radically different from what was undertaken.

interaction.prompt: Before Taylor v Caldwell, what was the position when performance of a contract became impossible through no fault of either party?
options: The promisor remained absolutely liable regardless of the impossibility
The contract was automatically void from the outset
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The old rule of absolute contractual liability held promisors to their bargain even where performance had become genuinely impossible — Taylor v Caldwell is precisely the case that softened this.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The pre-1863 position was harsher than voidness — it was absolute liability. A promisor who could not perform, however blamelessly, remained on the hook in damages until Taylor v Caldwell changed that.

parts.heading: Frustration of purpose: when performance is possible but pointless
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the coronation story before naming the wider principle
body: Taylor v Caldwell involved literal physical destruction — an easy case, in a sense, because performance was truly impossible. A harder question followed decades later: what if performance remains perfectly possible, but the entire commercial point of the contract has evaporated?

Krell v Henry supplies the answer. Mr Henry hired a room overlooking Pall Mall specifically to watch King Edward VII's coronation procession pass by — the flat was of no interest to him otherwise, and both parties understood the procession-viewing purpose, though the contract itself referred only to the hire of rooms for the two days. When the King fell ill and the procession was postponed, Henry refused to pay the balance of the hire fee. Krell sued.

The Court of Appeal held the contract was frustrated. Although the room was still physically available and Henry could still have occupied it, the entire foundation of the contract — its whole commercial purpose, known to and shared by both parties — had disappeared. Performing the letter of the contract while its point had vanished was, the court held, not what either party had bargained for.

This case is cited endlessly and misapplied almost as often. It does not mean a contract is frustrated whenever a party's personal motive for contracting fails. The purpose has to be the foundation of the contract itself, evident to both sides — not a private reason known only to one party. A companion case decided the same term, involving a boat hired to view a naval review that was then cancelled but where the boat could still be used for its ordinary purpose of cruising the fleet, went the other way, for exactly that reason.

components.factsShort: A room was hired specifically to view the coronation procession; the coronation was postponed due to the King's illness, though the room itself remained available.
components.ratioShort: A contract may be frustrated where its entire commercial purpose — known to and shared by both parties, though not stated as an express term — is destroyed, even if literal performance remains physically possible.

expanded.facts: Henry agreed to hire rooms from Krell overlooking the coronation procession route for two specific days, at a price reflecting the premium view. The written correspondence referred only to hire of the rooms, but the surrounding circumstances made the procession-viewing purpose obvious and mutually understood. The coronation was postponed when Edward VII required emergency surgery.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that the coronation procession was the foundation of the contract as both parties had understood it, even though not expressly stated as a term. Its non-occurrence deprived the contract of its entire substance, and the court would not hold Henry to paying for rooms that had become, in substance, worthless for the purpose both sides had in mind.
expanded.significance: Krell v Henry established that frustration can operate on frustration of purpose, not only physical or legal impossibility. It remains the leading illustration, but courts apply it cautiously — the shared purpose must be the foundation of the bargain, not a collateral motive of one party alone.

interaction.prompt: Which of these is more likely to be frustrated on Krell v Henry reasoning?
interaction.scenarioA: A function room is booked for a wedding reception, described throughout the booking correspondence as 'for the Smith-Jones wedding reception'; the wedding is called off.
interaction.scenarioB: A generic hotel room is booked for a weekend; the guest privately intended to attend a concert that weekend, never mentioned to the hotel, and the concert is cancelled.
interaction.explanation: In A, the shared, stated purpose known to both parties is the foundation of the booking, mirroring Krell v Henry. In B, the concert-attendance purpose was private to the guest and never part of the shared understanding, so its failure is simply an unfortunate personal circumstance, not a frustrating event.

parts.heading: Keeping the door narrow: hardship is not frustration
parts.voice: structural — sets out the modern test as a checklist against common wrong turns
body: If frustration excused parties every time a contract became harder, slower, or more expensive to perform than expected, commercial certainty would collapse — every party facing a bad bargain would simply claim frustration rather than absorb the loss or renegotiate. The courts have been resolutely strict about this, and the leading modern statement of the test comes from Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC.

A building contractor agreed a fixed price to build houses within eight months. Due to unexpected labour and materials shortages, entirely outside anyone's fault, the work took twenty-two months and cost far more than the contract price. The contractor argued the contract was frustrated and sought payment on a quantum meruit basis for the real value of the work, rather than being held to the fixed price.

The House of Lords rejected the claim. Lord Radcliffe formulated the now-standard test: frustration occurs when, without default of either party, a contractual obligation has become incapable of being performed because the circumstances in which performance is called for would render it a thing radically different from that which was undertaken by the contract. Delay and increased expense, however severe, were not enough — this was, in substance, an unusually bad bargain for the contractor, not a different contract altogether.

This case is the one to reach for whenever a fact pattern says a contract became slower, costlier, or less profitable than expected. Difficulty is not impossibility, and being a worse deal than either party hoped is not the same as being a radically different one.

components.label: Davis Contractors: the modern test, and what does NOT satisfy it
points: Test: performance must be rendered impossible, illegal, or radically different from what was undertaken, without default of either party
NOT enough: performance merely becomes more expensive or less profitable
NOT enough: performance is simply delayed, if the delay does not go to the root of the contract
NOT enough: one party has simply made a bad bargain that has turned out worse than hoped
The test is objective — assessed against what performance now actually requires, not against either party's subjective disappointment

interaction.prompt: A supplier's fixed-price contract becomes loss-making after raw material costs triple unexpectedly, though the supplier can still perform exactly as agreed. Is this frustration?
options: Yes — a threefold cost increase is clearly radical
No — increased expense alone, however severe, does not make performance radically different; the supplier has simply made a bad bargain
Yes — any unforeseen event outside either party's control is automatically frustrating
interaction.trapExplanation: A dramatic cost increase feels 'radical' in an everyday sense, which is exactly the trap. Davis Contractors is explicit that increased expense, however severe, does not by itself satisfy the test — performance itself must become a fundamentally different thing to perform, not merely a worse deal.

parts.heading: Two doors closed: self-induced frustration, and events foreseen
parts.voice: advisory — reads like a checklist of pitfalls given to a trainee before drafting an opinion
body: Two situations look, on the surface, like frustration but are firmly excluded, and examiners love both because they reward candidates who spot the exclusion rather than just the surface event.

First: self-induced frustration. A party cannot rely on frustration where the supervening event resulted, wholly or partly, from its own choice or default. The Super Servant Two illustrates this sharply. The defendants owned two heavy-lift transportation vessels, Super Servant One and Super Servant Two, and had contracted to transport a rig using 'one of the vessels', at their own election. Before performance, Super Servant Two sank. The defendants argued the contract was frustrated because their remaining vessel, Super Servant One, was already committed elsewhere. The Court of Appeal held this was not frustration: the defendants had chosen, by their own allocation decisions, to use Super Servant One for other contracts rather than this one — the impossibility flowed from their own election, not from the sinking alone. A party cannot engineer or contribute to the supervening event and then rely on it.

Second: events foreseen and provided for. If the parties actually anticipated the very event that occurred and made express provision for it — a force majeure clause allocating the risk, for instance — frustration has no role to play; the parties' own agreed allocation of that risk governs instead. Even where an event was reasonably foreseeable but not actually provided for, courts are more reluctant to find frustration, on the view that parties who could have protected themselves by contract but did not should generally bear the consequences of not doing so.

Canary Wharf v European Medicines Agency illustrates the courts' continued caution in a very modern setting. The EMA argued its lease was frustrated by the UK's withdrawal from the EU, since EU law required its headquarters to be within an EU member state. The High Court rejected the argument, holding that Brexit did not render performance of the lease radically different — the EMA could still occupy and use the premises, and in any event the possibility of Brexit was not so fundamentally unforeseeable, nor did it strike at the very basis of a long commercial lease, as to justify discharging it. The case is a useful modern data point confirming just how high the bar remains even for genuinely momentous supervening political events.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say the sinking of Super Servant Two was itself an unforeseen, blameless event, and conclude the contract must be frustrated.
components.whyItsWrong: The sinking was indeed blameless, but that was not the operative cause of non-performance. The defendants' own subsequent choice to allocate their one remaining vessel to other work is what actually made performance of this contract impossible — and a party cannot rely on frustration where its own election contributed to the impossibility.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that prevents the defendant relying on frustration in this scenario.
interaction.scenarioText: A haulage firm has two lorries and contracts to deliver goods for Client A using 'one of our lorries'. One lorry is destroyed in an accident. The firm then chooses to allocate its remaining lorry to a more profitable job for Client B instead, and tells Client A it cannot perform.
tappableSpans: contracts to deliver goods for Client A
one lorry is destroyed in an accident
chooses to allocate its remaining lorry to a more profitable job for Client B
tells Client A it cannot perform
interaction.correctSpan: chooses to allocate its remaining lorry to a more profitable job for Client B
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the self-inducing choice. The accident alone was blameless, but the firm's own subsequent election to use its surviving lorry elsewhere is what actually caused the failure to perform for Client A — mirroring The Super Servant Two.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The accident itself is not the problem — accidents happen without fault. Look for the moment the defendant makes a choice about how to use its remaining resources; that election is what defeats a frustration argument.

parts.heading: Cleaning up the mess: the 1943 Act
parts.voice: exam-focused — written as a direct problem-solving walkthrough for the statutory stage
body: Once a court finds frustration, the contract is automatically discharged from the moment of the frustrating event — but that leaves an obvious question: what happens to money already paid, work already done, or expenses already incurred before the event struck? The common law's original answer was crude and often unfair: money paid was simply irrecoverable, unless there had been a total failure of consideration. The Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 replaced that with a fairer statutory scheme, and it is worth being able to apply section by section rather than just naming it.

Section 1(2) deals with money: sums paid before the frustrating event are recoverable, and sums due but not yet paid cease to be payable. But the court has discretion to allow the payee to retain, or recover, expenses it incurred in performance before the frustrating event, up to the value of those expenses — so a party is not left having spent money in reliance on the contract with literally nothing to show for it, even though it must give back sums that go beyond that.

Section 1(3) deals with non-money benefits: where one party has obtained a valuable benefit (other than a payment of money) from the other's performance before the frustrating event, the court may order it to pay a just sum in respect of that benefit — capped at the value of the benefit actually received, assessed in light of the frustrating event's effect on that value, not at the cost of providing it.

Applying this to an exam problem is mostly a matter of working through the sequence methodically: identify the frustrating event and its date; identify all payments made and due up to that point (section 1(2)); identify any expenses either party incurred in reliance before that date, which a court may allow to be retained or recovered out of those payments; then identify any non-money valuable benefit conferred on the other party before that date (section 1(3)) and value it fairly. Certain contracts — including specific goods contracts already governed by the Sale of Goods Act's own frustration rules, and some insurance and charterparty contracts — are excluded from the 1943 Act by its own terms, which is worth flagging rather than assuming the Act always applies.

components.text: (2) All sums paid or payable to any party in pursuance of the contract before the time of discharge shall, in the case of sums so paid, be recoverable from him as money received by him for the use of the party by whom the sums were paid, and, in the case of sums so payable, cease to be so payable: Provided that the court may allow the payee to retain or recover expenses incurred before discharge, up to the value of those expenses. (3) Where any party has obtained a valuable benefit (other than a payment of money) before discharge, the court may require him to pay a just sum, not exceeding the value of the benefit, having regard to the effect of the circumstances giving rise to the frustration.
elements: Sums paid before discharge are prima facie recoverable
Sums due but unpaid cease to be payable
Court discretion to allow retention/recovery of reliance expenses, capped at their value
Court discretion to award a just sum for a non-money valuable benefit, capped at its value as affected by the frustrating event

interaction.prompt: A client pays a wedding photographer a £2,000 deposit for a booking six months out. The photographer spends £600 on non-refundable equipment hire specifically for this booking. Four months before the wedding, new emergency legislation makes the planned venue unlawful to use for any function, and the wedding cannot proceed anywhere in time. Applying the 1943 Act, what is the likely outcome regarding the £2,000?
factsToOrder: £2,000 deposit paid before the frustrating event
Legislation makes the venue unlawful — a frustrating event (impossibility/illegality)
Photographer incurred £600 in reliance expenses before discharge
Court has discretion under s 1(2) to allow retention of expenses up to their value

scaffolds.support: Guided single-step answer with the statutory reasoning shown

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the client can recover the £2,000 deposit, and whether the photographer can retain any part of it for expenses incurred.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 1(2) of the 1943 Act makes sums paid before discharge prima facie recoverable, but allows the court discretion to permit the payee to retain or recover expenses incurred in performance before the frustrating event, capped at the value of those expenses.
modelAnswer.application: The new legislation renders the booking impossible to perform as agreed, a frustrating event. The £2,000 was paid before that event, so it is prima facie recoverable by the client. However, the photographer incurred £600 in reliance expenses before discharge, and the court may exercise its discretion to allow the photographer to retain up to that £600 out of the deposit.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The client is likely to recover £1,400, with the photographer permitted to retain up to £600 to cover reliance expenses actually incurred.

testPool.prompt: State the modern test for frustration as formulated in Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC.
acceptableAnswers: radically different performance without default of either party
performance has become impossible, illegal, or radically different from what was undertaken
testPool.modelAnswer: Frustration occurs where, without the default of either party, a contractual obligation has become incapable of being performed because the circumstances would render performance a thing radically different from that undertaken by the contract.

testPool.prompt: Which case first established the doctrine of frustration, on facts involving destruction of a music hall?
options: Taylor v Caldwell
Krell v Henry

testPool.prompt: Which of the following will NOT, without more, amount to frustration?
options: Physical destruction of the specific subject matter of the contract
Supervening illegality of the whole method of performance
A fixed-price contract simply becoming significantly more expensive to perform than expected
testPool.trapExplanation: Increased expense alone does not satisfy the 'radically different' test from Davis Contractors, however severe — the courts treat this as an ordinary commercial risk, not a frustrating event.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps a court follows in analysing a frustration claim.
items: Identify the supervening event and confirm it occurred without either party's fault
Ask whether performance is now impossible, illegal, or radically different from what was undertaken
Check the event was not self-induced by the party seeking to rely on it
Check the event was not one the parties foresaw and provided for
If frustration is established, apply the 1943 Act to unwind payments, expenses, and benefits

testPool.prompt: Under s 1(3) of the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943, what is the cap on a 'just sum' awarded for a non-money valuable benefit?
options: The value of the benefit actually received, having regard to the effect of the frustrating event on that value
The full cost the provider incurred in conferring the benefit, regardless of its value to the recipient
There is no cap

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from The Super Servant Two, highlight the sentence stating why the defence of frustration failed.
testPool.passage: The defendants owned two vessels and had a contractual option as to which to use. One vessel sank through no fault of the defendants. The defendants then chose to deploy their remaining vessel on other contracts rather than this one. Frustration cannot be relied upon where the alleged frustrating event results from an election made by the party seeking to rely on it. The claim of frustration therefore failed.
testPool.ratioSentence: Frustration cannot be relied upon where the alleged frustrating event results from an election made by the party seeking to rely on it.

testPool.prompt: A concert venue is booked for a specific band's performance, described throughout as such in the booking. The band splits up acrimoniously before the date and cannot perform. Is the booking contract likely frustrated?
options: Yes — the shared, stated foundation of the contract (that specific band's performance) has been destroyed, mirroring Krell v Henry
No — frustration never applies to entertainment bookings
No — the venue itself remains available, so nothing has changed
testPool.explanation: As in Krell v Henry, the contract's foundation — here, the specific band's performance, known to and shared by both parties — has disappeared, even though the physical venue remains available and usable in the abstract.

testPool.prompt: A shipping contract includes an express force majeure clause allocating the risk of port closures due to war. A war does close the relevant port. Can either party claim frustration instead of relying on the clause?
options: No — where the parties foresaw and expressly provided for the event, their own risk allocation governs and frustration has no role
Yes — war always frustrates shipping contracts regardless of any clause
Yes — frustration and force majeure clauses always operate side by side automatically
testPool.explanation: Frustration is a doctrine of last resort for genuinely unprovided-for events. Where the parties foresaw the very risk and allocated it by an express clause, that clause governs and frustration is excluded.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most undermines a claim that this lease was frustrated.
testPool.scenarioText: A tenant leases office premises for ten years. Several years in, new legislation changes commuting patterns in the area, and the tenant argues the lease is frustrated because fewer staff now want to work from that location, making the lease commercially disappointing. The tenant can still lawfully occupy and use the premises exactly as before.
tappableSpans: leases office premises for ten years
can still lawfully occupy and use the premises exactly as before
testPool.correctSpan: can still lawfully occupy and use the premises exactly as before
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Where performance — here, lawful occupation and use of the premises — remains entirely possible and unchanged in substance, a mere drop in commercial desirability is a bad bargain, not a radically different obligation, echoing the reasoning in Canary Wharf v EMA.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on whether performance itself has changed, not on whether the deal has become less attractive. The tenant can still do exactly what the lease requires — that fact is fatal to a frustration argument.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is more likely to be self-induced frustration, barring the defence?
testPool.scenarioA: A specialist machine essential to performance is destroyed by an unforeseeable factory fire with no negligence by anyone.
testPool.scenarioB: A supplier with only one relevant production line chooses to prioritise a more lucrative rival order on that line, making it late in a way it says makes the original contract 'impossible' to perform on time.
testPool.explanation: In B, the supplier's own commercial choice to prioritise another contract is what produces the impossibility — a party cannot rely on frustration where its own election contributed to it, as in The Super Servant Two. A is a genuinely external, blameless event.

testPool.prompt: A buyer has paid a £5,000 deposit under a contract later found to be frustrated, and the seller had incurred no expenses at all before discharge. What happens to the £5,000 under s 1(2) of the 1943 Act?
options: It is recoverable by the buyer in full, since no expenses were incurred to justify any retention
It is always kept in full by the seller regardless of expenses

testPool.prompt: An events company contracts to cater an outdoor festival on a fixed date, at a fixed price, with £3,000 paid upfront. Three weeks before the event, the local authority bans all outdoor gatherings above 50 people for the whole region due to a sudden public health emergency, and the ban is confirmed to remain in force through the festival date. The organiser had already spent £900 on perishable ingredients that are now wasted. Analyse the legal consequences.
factsToOrder: The ban is imposed by the local authority for public health reasons, with no fault on either party
The ban covers the whole event and remains in force through the festival date
£3,000 was paid upfront before the ban
£900 was spent on now-wasted perishable ingredients before the ban

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the contract is frustrated by the ban, and if so, what happens to the £3,000 paid and the £900 spent.
modelAnswer.rule: A contract is frustrated where a supervening event, without either party's fault, renders performance impossible, illegal, or radically different from what was undertaken (Davis Contractors). Where frustration is established, s 1(2) of the 1943 Act makes sums paid before discharge prima facie recoverable, subject to the court's discretion to allow the payee to retain or recover reliance expenses incurred before discharge, up to their value.
modelAnswer.application: The ban makes the agreed outdoor catering for this event legally impossible for the whole relevant period, with no fault on either party — this is a genuine frustrating event, not mere hardship or increased cost. The £3,000 was paid before the frustrating event and is therefore prima facie recoverable by the organiser under s 1(2). However, the events company incurred £900 in reliance expenses before discharge, and a court may exercise its discretion to allow the events company to retain up to that £900 from the deposit.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The contract is frustrated; the organiser can likely recover £2,100 of the £3,000, with the events company permitted to retain up to £900 for its wasted expenses.

testPool.prompt: Why did the court in Canary Wharf v European Medicines Agency reject the frustration argument based on Brexit?
options: Because Brexit was legally impossible to have foreseen at the time the lease was signed

Because the EMA could still occupy and use the premises, and the possibility of such a political change was not so fundamentally unforeseeable or basis-destroying as to justify discharge of a long commercial lease
Because frustration can never apply to leases under any circumstances
testPool.trapExplanation: Frustration can in principle apply to leases in extreme cases; the court did not rule it out categorically. The actual reasoning turned on performance remaining possible and the change not striking at the basis of the bargain in the way the doctrine requires.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating hardship, delay, or increased expense as if it were automatically frustrating. Always ask: has performance become radically different, or has it just become a worse deal?
